case: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of an 18-month history of shaking of his right hand and slowness in daily tasks. His handwriting has become small, and his wife says his face looks expressionless. He takes no medications. Physical examination shows a 4 to 5 Hz pill-rolling tremor of the right hand that is present at rest and lessens when he reaches for an object. There is cogwheel rigidity of the right arm, slow finger tapping, reduced arm swing on the right, and a stooped, shuffling gait. Strength, sensation, and reflexes are normal. MRI of the brain shows only age-appropriate changes. Diagnosis: idiopathic Parkinson disease.

questions.stem: Eight years later, he dies of aspiration pneumonia. Which of the following findings is most likely on examination of his brain at autopsy?
options: Caudate atrophy with intranuclear huntingtin aggregates
Anterior horn cell loss with TDP-43 cytoplasmic inclusions
Nigral depigmentation with alpha-synuclein inclusions
Frontotemporal atrophy with round tau inclusions in neurons
approach: Link resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia to loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
Recall the inclusion that marks these neurons: the Lewy body, made of alpha-synuclein.
Match the other options to Huntington disease, ALS, and frontotemporal dementia.
questions.why: Parkinson disease destroys the pigmented dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta, so the midbrain looks pale at autopsy. Surviving neurons contain Lewy bodies, round eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions made mostly of alpha-synuclein. Symptoms appear after most nigral neurons are gone. Secondary parkinsonism looks similar clinically but has a different cause, such as the toxin MPTP, which kills nigral neurons, or dopamine D2 blockers such as haloperidol and metoclopramide.
whyNot: This is Huntington disease, which causes chorea and dementia, with atrophy of the caudate nucleus.
This is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which causes weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs. His strength is normal.
Correct.
Round tau inclusions (Pick bodies) mark one form of frontotemporal dementia, which begins with behavior or language change instead of a movement disorder.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in basal ganglia circuitry most directly explains his bradykinesia?
options: Increased inhibitory output from the internal globus pallidus to the thalamus
Decreased activity of the subthalamic nucleus driving the internal globus pallidus
Increased activity of direct pathway striatal neurons bearing D1 receptors
Decreased activity of indirect pathway striatal neurons bearing D2 receptors
approach: Recall that nigral dopamine excites the direct pathway through D1 receptors and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2 receptors.
With dopamine lost, the direct pathway falls and the indirect pathway rises; both changes increase internal pallidal output.
More inhibitory pallidal output to the thalamus means less excitation of motor cortex, so movement is slow and small.
questions.why: The internal globus pallidus (GPi) tonically inhibits the motor thalamus with GABA. The direct pathway (striatum to GPi) suppresses the GPi and releases movement, and dopamine strengthens it through D1 receptors. The indirect pathway (striatum to external pallidus to subthalamic nucleus to GPi) increases GPi output, and dopamine weakens it through D2 receptors. When nigral dopamine is lost, both effects push GPi output up, the thalamus is held down, and the cortex gets too little drive to start and scale movement.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of dopamine releases the indirect pathway, so the subthalamic nucleus becomes overactive. That is why deep brain stimulation of this nucleus can help.
Direct pathway neurons lose their D1 excitation, so their activity falls. Increased direct pathway activity would produce excess movement.
Indirect pathway neurons lose their D2 inhibition, so their activity rises. Reduced indirect pathway activity is what happens in early Huntington disease and causes chorea.

topics: Direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways

questions.stem: The neurons lost in his disease share their neurotransmitter with a second group of midbrain neurons that projects to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex. In which of the following nuclei are those neurons located?
options: Nucleus basalis of Meynert
Locus coeruleus
Dorsal raphe nucleus
Ventral tegmental area
approach: Name the transmitter of the neurons lost in Parkinson disease: dopamine.
Recall the two main dopamine source nuclei in the midbrain: substantia nigra pars compacta and the ventral tegmental area.
The ventral tegmental area supplies the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways.
questions.why: Dopamine neurons sit in two neighboring midbrain groups. The substantia nigra pars compacta sends the nigrostriatal pathway to the caudate and putamen, and its loss causes the motor signs of Parkinson disease. The ventral tegmental area sends the mesolimbic pathway to the nucleus accumbens and the mesocortical pathway to prefrontal cortex, which handle reward and motivation. A third dopamine group, in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, inhibits prolactin release.
whyNot: This basal forebrain nucleus is the main source of cortical acetylcholine. It degenerates in Alzheimer disease.
The locus coeruleus in the pons is the main source of norepinephrine in the brain.
The raphe nuclei of the brainstem are the main source of serotonin.
Correct.

questions.stem: His 59-year-old sister has a 10-year history of tremor of both hands that makes it hard to hold a cup of coffee. The tremor lessens after a glass of wine. Their late mother had a similar tremor. Examination shows a symmetric 7 Hz tremor of the outstretched hands that is absent with the arms at rest and does not increase as her finger nears the target on finger-to-nose testing. Tone, finger tapping speed, and gait are normal. Serum TSH is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in the sister?
options: Cerebellar intention tremor
Essential tremor
Parkinsonian resting tremor
Enhanced physiologic tremor
approach: Classify the tremor by when it appears: with posture and action, absent at rest.
Check for features of other tremors: no increase near the target (cerebellar), no rigidity or bradykinesia (parkinsonian).
A long-standing, familial, alcohol-responsive action tremor is essential tremor.
questions.why: Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder in adults. It is a postural and action tremor of both hands that often runs in families in an autosomal dominant pattern and often improves briefly with alcohol. It may also involve the head or voice. Parkinsonian tremor occurs at rest and comes with rigidity and bradykinesia, as in her brother. Cerebellar tremor gets worse as the hand approaches a target.
whyNot: Cerebellar intention tremor grows as the finger approaches the target and comes with ataxia and dysmetria. Her tremor does not change near the target.
Correct.
Parkinsonian tremor is present at rest and lessens with action. Her tremor is absent at rest, and tone and finger tapping are normal.

Enhanced physiologic tremor is a fine postural tremor driven by adrenergic excess, such as hyperthyroidism, caffeine, or anxiety. A 10-year familial course with a normal TSH fits essential tremor better.

case: A 41-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband because of a 2-year history of irritability, low mood, forgetfulness, and restless, fidgety movements. She has lost her job as a bookkeeper because of errors. Her father developed similar symptoms at the age of 48 years and died at the age of 60 years. Physical examination shows brief, irregular, flowing movements of the face, trunk, and fingers. She cannot keep her tongue protruded or maintain a steady hand grip. Saccadic eye movements are slow. MRI of the brain shows atrophy of the caudate nuclei with enlarged frontal horns of the lateral ventricles. Genetic testing shows 44 CAG repeats in one HTT allele (normal 26 or fewer). Diagnosis: Huntington disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following neuronal populations is most severely lost in the atrophic structures seen on her MRI?
options: Dopaminergic neurons of the pars compacta
GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the striatum
Cholinergic neurons of the basal nucleus of Meynert
Glutamatergic neurons of the subthalamic nucleus
approach: Identify the atrophic structure: the caudate nucleus, part of the striatum.
Recall that most striatal neurons are GABAergic medium spiny neurons.
Link early loss of indirect pathway medium spiny neurons to chorea.
questions.why: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4p. Mutant huntingtin injures striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurons first, so the caudate and then the putamen atrophy and the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles look enlarged. Indirect pathway neurons are lost early, which releases the thalamus and produces chorea. Cortical neuron loss adds dementia, depression, and personality change, usually starting at the age of 30 to 50 years.
whyNot: These neurons are lost in Parkinson disease, which causes resting tremor and bradykinesia instead of chorea.
Correct.
These cholinergic neurons are lost in Alzheimer disease. They lie in the basal forebrain, not in the caudate.
A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus, usually a small stroke, causes hemiballismus on the opposite side. It is not the structure that atrophies in this disease.

questions.stem: Her father's symptoms began at the age of 48 years, and hers began at the age of 39 years. Which of the following best explains her earlier onset?
options: Maternal imprinting of the normal HTT allele
Mitochondrial heteroplasmy in striatal neurons
Somatic mosaicism from a postzygotic mutation
Paternal meiotic expansion of the CAG repeat
approach: Recognize anticipation: earlier onset and more severe disease in each generation.
Recall that anticipation in trinucleotide repeat disorders comes from further expansion of the repeat when it is passed on.
In Huntington disease the CAG repeat is most unstable in spermatogenesis, so expansion is most likely when the father passes it on.
questions.why: Huntington disease is one of the trinucleotide repeat disorders. A longer CAG repeat gives earlier onset, and the repeat tends to lengthen when transmitted, most of all through the father's sperm. This produces anticipation. Myotonic dystrophy (CTG in DMPK, autosomal dominant) and fragile X syndrome (CGG in FMR1, X-linked) also show anticipation, but there expansion happens mainly in maternal transmission. Friedreich ataxia (GAA in the frataxin gene) is autosomal recessive.
whyNot: Imprinting silences one parent's allele and underlies Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes. HTT is not imprinted, and the disease is caused by a toxic gain of function from the mutant allele.
Heteroplasmy explains variable severity in mitochondrial DNA disorders, which pass only from the mother. Her disease came from her father and the gene is nuclear.
Postzygotic mosaicism explains patchy disease in one person, such as McCune-Albright syndrome. It does not explain earlier onset across generations.
Correct.

questions.stem: The neurons lost in her striatum make their main neurotransmitter from glutamate in a single enzymatic step. Which of the following cofactors is required for this reaction?
options: Pyridoxal phosphate
Tetrahydrobiopterin
Thiamine pyrophosphate
S-adenosylmethionine
approach: Identify the transmitter of striatal medium spiny neurons: GABA.
Recall that GABA is made by decarboxylation of glutamate by glutamate decarboxylase.
Amino acid decarboxylases use pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6.
questions.why: Glutamate decarboxylase removes the carboxyl group of glutamate to form GABA, and it needs pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6). Severe B6 deficiency, as from isoniazid without supplementation, lowers GABA and can cause seizures. Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter and acts on NMDA and AMPA receptors, while GABA and glycine are inhibitory. Too much glutamate drives calcium into neurons through NMDA receptors and kills them, which is excitotoxicity, a mechanism in ischemic neuronal death and thought to contribute to striatal loss in Huntington disease.
whyNot: Correct.
Tetrahydrobiopterin is the cofactor for phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylases, which start catecholamine and serotonin synthesis.
Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
S-adenosylmethionine donates methyl groups, as in the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine. It is not used to make GABA.

questions.stem: The structure that is atrophic on her MRI forms the lateral wall of the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. From which of the following embryonic brain vesicles does this structure develop?
options: Diencephalon
Mesencephalon
Telencephalon
Metencephalon
approach: Identify the structure: the head of the caudate nucleus.
Recall that the basal nuclei, cerebral hemispheres, and lateral ventricles all come from the telencephalon.
Exclude vesicles that form the thalamus, midbrain, and pons.
questions.why: The prosencephalon divides into the telencephalon and diencephalon. The telencephalon forms the cerebral cortex, the basal nuclei including the caudate and putamen, and the lateral ventricles, so the caudate grows around the wall of the lateral ventricle. The diencephalon forms the thalamus, hypothalamus, and third ventricle. The mesencephalon forms the midbrain and cerebral aqueduct, the metencephalon forms the pons and cerebellum, and the myelencephalon forms the medulla, with the fourth ventricle spanning the last two.
whyNot: The diencephalon forms the thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, and third ventricle. The thalamus lies medial to the internal capsule, not at the frontal horn.
The mesencephalon forms the midbrain, including the substantia nigra, and the cerebral aqueduct.
Correct.
The metencephalon forms the pons and cerebellum and the upper part of the fourth ventricle.

dx: Guillain-Barre syndrome after Campylobacter jejuni enteritis
case: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 4 days of tingling in his feet and progressive weakness that began in his legs and now involves his arms. Three weeks ago he had 4 days of bloody diarrhea, and a stool culture grew Campylobacter jejuni. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg; over the next hour, blood pressure falls to 102/60 mm Hg. Strength is 3/5 in the legs and 4/5 in the arms, symmetric. Deep tendon reflexes are absent. Forced vital capacity is 2.6 L (predicted 4.6 L). Cerebrospinal fluid shows a protein concentration of 160 mg/dL (15 to 45) and 2 leukocytes/µL (0 to 5). Nerve conduction studies show slowed conduction and conduction block. Diagnosis: Guillain-Barre syndrome.

questions.stem: Over the next 24 hours, his forced vital capacity falls to 1.2 L, and he can no longer count to 10 in one breath. Which of the following best explains this change?
options: Demyelination of the medullary respiratory centers
Antibody blockade of diaphragmatic acetylcholine receptors
Degeneration of cervical anterior horn motor neurons
Demyelination of the phrenic and intercostal nerves
approach: Recognize that Guillain-Barre syndrome attacks peripheral nerve myelin, including nerve roots and proximal nerves.
Apply this to breathing: the diaphragm and intercostal muscles are driven by the phrenic and intercostal nerves.
A falling vital capacity means neuromuscular respiratory failure, the main cause of death in this disease.
questions.why: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. It causes ascending, symmetric, flaccid weakness with lost reflexes. When the phrenic nerves (C3 to C5) and intercostal nerves are involved, the respiratory muscles weaken and vital capacity falls, so serial vital capacity is followed and patients are intubated before they tire. Involvement of autonomic fibers causes swings in blood pressure and heart rate, as in this patient, and arrhythmias.
whyNot: Guillain-Barre syndrome affects the peripheral nervous system. Central demyelination of the brainstem occurs in multiple sclerosis and osmotic demyelination, not here.
Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, which gives fatigable weakness with normal reflexes and normal CSF.
Loss of anterior horn cells occurs in ALS and poliomyelitis. It does not produce high CSF protein with slowed nerve conduction.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how his recent infection led to his neurologic illness?
options: Exotoxin carried retrogradely up motor axons
Antibodies to bacterial glycans that bind gangliosides
Direct bacterial invasion of dorsal root ganglia
Superantigen activation of T cells that attack central myelin
approach: Note the timing: weakness began weeks after the diarrhea cleared, which suggests an immune response, not ongoing infection.
Recall that Campylobacter jejuni lipooligosaccharide resembles gangliosides on peripheral nerve.
Antibodies made against the bacterium cross-react with the nerve, which is molecular mimicry.
questions.why: Campylobacter jejuni is the infection most often linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome. Its lipooligosaccharide looks like human gangliosides such as GM1 and GD1a. Antibodies raised against the bacterium bind these gangliosides on peripheral nerve myelin or axons, fix complement, and recruit macrophages that strip myelin. The Miller Fisher variant, with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, is tied to anti-GQ1b antibodies, because GQ1b is rich in the nerves to the eye muscles.
whyNot: Retrograde axonal transport of a toxin describes tetanus toxin, which blocks inhibitory interneurons and causes spastic paralysis, not flaccid weakness.
Correct.
The infection was confined to the gut and had cleared. The CSF has almost no leukocytes, which argues against active infection near the nerve roots.
Superantigens from Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes cause toxic shock. This disease attacks peripheral myelin, not central myelin.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why loss of myelin slows conduction along his motor nerves?
options: Reduced axon diameter from loss of neurofilaments
Prolonged refractory period of nodal sodium channels
Current leak and higher capacitance along the internodes
Hyperpolarization of the axon resting membrane potential
approach: Recall that myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance between nodes of Ranvier.
This lets current spread quickly to the next node, which is saltatory conduction.
Without myelin, current leaks out and charges more membrane, so the next node reaches threshold late or not at all.
questions.why: In a myelinated axon, sodium channels cluster at the nodes of Ranvier, and the insulated internode carries current passively and quickly to the next node. Demyelination lowers membrane resistance and raises capacitance, so current leaks away and more charge is needed to change the voltage. Conduction slows, and if too little current reaches the next node, conduction fails, which is conduction block. The bare internode has few sodium channels, so it cannot generate its own action potential well. Larger diameter axons conduct faster because their internal resistance is lower.
whyNot: Axon diameter does affect speed, but demyelination does not shrink the axon. The defect here is in the myelin sheath.
The refractory period limits how fast an axon can fire repeatedly. It is not the reason a single impulse travels slowly after demyelination.
Correct.
Demyelination does not change the resting membrane potential. Hyperpolarization would reduce excitability by a different mechanism, as with low extracellular potassium.

questions.stem: Electrodiagnostic testing 3 weeks later shows that some motor axons in his legs were also severed by the inflammation, with Wallerian degeneration distal to the injury. Which of the following best explains why these axons can regrow while severed axons in the spinal cord generally cannot?
options: Schwann cells form guiding tubes and secrete growth factors
Oligodendrocytes clear myelin debris and guide new sprouts
Mature motor neurons divide to replace the injured neurons
Astrocytes form a permissive scar bridging the damaged segment
approach: Recall Wallerian degeneration: the axon and myelin distal to the injury break down and are cleared by macrophages.
In peripheral nerve, Schwann cells survive inside the endoneurial tube and make growth factors and adhesion molecules.
In the CNS, oligodendrocyte myelin inhibitors and the astrocytic glial scar block regrowth.
questions.why: After an axon is cut, the distal segment and its myelin degenerate (Wallerian degeneration), and the cell body swells with a displaced nucleus and dispersed Nissl substance (central chromatolysis). In peripheral nerve, Schwann cells multiply within the intact basal lamina tube, secrete nerve growth factors, and guide sprouts from the proximal stump at about 1 to 3 mm per day. In the CNS, macrophages clear debris slowly, oligodendrocyte myelin proteins such as Nogo inhibit growth, and astrocytes form a glial scar.
whyNot: Correct.
Oligodendrocytes are CNS cells. Their myelin contains proteins that inhibit axon growth, which is one reason CNS axons fail to regenerate.
Neurons are postmitotic and do not divide. Recovery depends on regrowth of the axon from the surviving cell body.
Astrocytes are CNS cells, and their scar blocks regrowth. Peripheral nerves contain no astrocytes.

dx: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis with trigeminal neuralgia
case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 6 weeks of brief, electric shock-like pains in her left cheek and jaw that last a few seconds and are set off by brushing her teeth or chewing. She also has double vision when she looks to the right. Two years ago she had blurred, painful vision in her right eye that resolved over 6 weeks. Her symptoms feel worse after a hot shower. On rightward gaze, the left eye does not adduct, and the right eye shows nystagmus as it abducts. Convergence is normal. Facial sensation is normal between attacks. MRI shows multiple ovoid T2-hyperintense lesions oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles and a lesion in the left pons. Cerebrospinal fluid shows oligoclonal IgG bands absent from serum. Diagnosis: relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis with trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her symptoms worsen after a hot shower?
options: Heat worsens conduction block in demyelinated axons
Heat triggers a new inflammatory plaque within hours
Heat dilates cerebral vessels and raises intracranial pressure
Heat lowers acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
approach: Recognize the Uhthoff phenomenon: brief worsening of old symptoms with a rise in body temperature.
Recall that demyelinated axons conduct with very little safety margin.
Higher temperature shortens sodium channel opening, so less current reaches the next node and conduction fails.
questions.why: Multiple sclerosis most often affects women aged 20 to 40 years and is more common at higher latitudes. Its typical course is relapsing-remitting, with attacks such as optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, sensory loss, and weakness that improve over weeks. Heat speeds sodium channel inactivation, which reduces the current available at each node. A demyelinated axon already barely reaches threshold, so a small rise in temperature can block conduction. The worsening reverses with cooling and does not mean new disease activity.
whyNot: Correct.
Heat-related worsening comes on within minutes and reverses with cooling. A true relapse from a new plaque lasts at least 24 hours and is not triggered by a shower.
Intracranial pressure is not raised in multiple sclerosis, and raised pressure would not reproduce her old focal symptoms.
Heat-sensitive neuromuscular weakness is not a feature of this disease. Multiple sclerosis affects central myelin, not the neuromuscular junction.

questions.stem: Which of the following immune effectors is most directly responsible for initiating the lesions seen on her MRI?
options: Antibodies against astrocyte aquaporin-4 channels
Antibodies against peripheral nerve gangliosides
CD4 Th1 and Th17 cells reactive to CNS myelin
Th2 cells driving IgE-mediated mast cell injury
approach: Identify the lesions as periventricular demyelinating plaques in the CNS.
Recall that multiple sclerosis is driven by autoreactive CD4 T cells against myelin proteins.
Th1 cells make interferon-gamma and Th17 cells make IL-17, which recruit macrophages that strip myelin.
questions.why: In multiple sclerosis, CD4 T cells reactive to myelin antigens such as myelin basic protein cross the blood-brain barrier. Th1 cells secrete interferon-gamma and activate macrophages and microglia, and Th17 cells secrete IL-17 and recruit neutrophils and other inflammatory cells. Together they destroy myelin and oligodendrocytes around venules, which is why plaques line up perpendicular to the ventricles. B cells inside the CNS make the oligoclonal IgG bands. The strongest genetic risk is HLA-DR2 (DRB1*15:01).
whyNot: Antibodies to aquaporin-4 cause neuromyelitis optica, with severe optic neuritis and long spinal cord lesions. That is a separate disease from multiple sclerosis.
Anti-ganglioside antibodies attack peripheral nerve in Guillain-Barre syndrome. Her lesions are in the brain.
Correct.
Th2 and IgE responses drive allergy and defense against parasites. They do not cause demyelinating plaques.

questions.stem: Damage to which of the following structures best explains her abnormal eye movements?
options: Right abducens nucleus
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Left oculomotor nerve
Right paramedian pontine reticular formation
approach: Note the pattern: the left eye fails to adduct on right gaze, but convergence is intact.
Intact convergence shows the left medial rectus and its nerve work, so the defect is in the pathway that links the two eyes during lateral gaze.
This link is the medial longitudinal fasciculus, which runs from the right abducens nucleus to the left oculomotor nucleus.
questions.why: For rightward gaze, the right paramedian pontine reticular formation activates the right abducens nucleus. Its motor neurons move the right lateral rectus, and its interneurons cross and ascend in the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the left oculomotor nucleus for the left medial rectus. A lesion of the left MLF blocks only this signal, so the left eye fails to adduct, and the right eye shows nystagmus as it abducts. Convergence uses a separate pathway, so it is preserved. This internuclear ophthalmoplegia is classic for multiple sclerosis in a young adult, and bilateral INO strongly suggests it.
whyNot: A right abducens nucleus lesion causes a right horizontal gaze palsy, with neither eye able to look to the right.
Correct.
A left oculomotor nerve lesion would also impair convergence and would cause ptosis, a dilated pupil, and a down-and-out eye.
A right paramedian pontine reticular formation lesion prevents both eyes from moving to the right.

questions.stem: Her facial pain is attributed to a demyelinating plaque at the trigeminal root entry zone in the pons. In a 68-year-old man without multiple sclerosis who has identical attacks, which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Reactivated varicella-zoster virus in the trigeminal ganglion
Tumor at the cerebellopontine angle
Arthritis of the temporomandibular joint
Arterial loop compressing the trigeminal root
approach: Recognize trigeminal neuralgia: seconds-long, one-sided, stabbing pain in V2 or V3, triggered by touch or chewing, with normal sensation between attacks.
In older adults it is usually caused by a blood vessel pressing on the nerve root near the pons.
In a young adult, the same syndrome raises concern for multiple sclerosis, as in this patient.
questions.why: Classic trigeminal neuralgia comes from compression of the trigeminal root near where it enters the pons, most often by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery. The pressure causes focal demyelination, and impulses jump between neighboring fibers, so light touch triggers bursts of pain. A plaque at the same site causes the same pain in multiple sclerosis. First-line drug treatment is carbamazepine, and decompression surgery can move the vessel off the nerve.
whyNot: Herpes zoster in the trigeminal territory causes a vesicular rash, most often in V1, and steady burning pain afterward. It does not cause brief triggered shocks with normal skin.
A cerebellopontine angle tumor can cause facial pain, but it is a less common cause and usually brings sensory loss, hearing loss, or other cranial nerve signs.
Temporomandibular joint disease causes aching jaw pain with chewing and joint tenderness or clicking. It does not cause electric shock-like pain triggered by light touch.
Correct.

case: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician because of recurrent episodes of spinning vertigo over the past 8 months. Each episode lasts 2 to 4 hours and comes with nausea, vomiting, a roaring sound, and a feeling of fullness in the left ear. Hearing in the left ear seems muffled during episodes and partly recovers between them. He feels well between episodes and has had no recent infections. Examination between episodes shows normal tympanic membranes and no nystagmus. Audiometry shows sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear, worst at low frequencies. MRI of the internal auditory canals is normal. Diagnosis: Meniere disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality in his left inner ear?
options: Overproduction of perilymph by the cochlear aqueduct
Loss of outer hair cells at the cochlear base
Poor endolymph resorption by the endolymphatic sac
Perilymph leakage through a round window fistula
approach: Recall the two inner ear fluids: potassium-rich endolymph in the membranous labyrinth and sodium-rich perilymph around it.
Endolymph is made by the stria vascularis and absorbed by the endolymphatic sac.
Meniere disease is endolymphatic hydrops: too much endolymph, thought to come mainly from poor resorption, distends the cochlear duct and vestibular organs.
questions.why: In Meniere disease, the volume of endolymph rises and distends the membranous labyrinth. Distension of the cochlear duct disturbs hair cell function at the low-frequency apex first, giving fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus, and fullness. Episodes of distension, and possibly small ruptures that let potassium-rich endolymph mix with perilymph, are thought to disturb the vestibular hair cells and cause vertigo lasting hours. With repeated attacks, hearing loss can become permanent.
whyNot: Perilymph communicates with the subarachnoid space through the cochlear aqueduct. Excess perilymph is not the mechanism of this disease.
Loss of basal outer hair cells causes high-frequency loss, as in noise exposure and presbycusis, without episodic vertigo.
Correct.
A perilymph fistula usually follows barotrauma or straining and causes sudden hearing loss with vertigo triggered by pressure changes.

questions.stem: Which of the following tuning fork results is most likely in this patient?
options: Weber lateralizes to the left ear; bone conduction exceeds air conduction in the left ear
Weber is midline; bone conduction exceeds air conduction in both ears
Weber lateralizes to the left ear; air conduction exceeds bone conduction in both ears
Weber lateralizes to the right ear; air conduction exceeds bone conduction in both ears
approach: Classify the loss: sensorineural, in the left ear.
In sensorineural loss, the Weber sound lateralizes to the better ear, here the right.
In sensorineural loss, the Rinne test stays normal, with air conduction better than bone conduction.
questions.why: Sound normally travels through the tympanic membrane and ossicles to the oval window, which is why air conduction is louder than bone conduction (a positive Rinne test). In conductive loss, bone conduction exceeds air conduction in the affected ear, and the Weber tone lateralizes to that ear. In sensorineural loss, the affected cochlea or nerve responds poorly to both routes, so the Rinne test stays normal and the Weber tone lateralizes to the healthy ear. Hair cells in the base of the cochlea respond to high frequencies and those at the apex to low frequencies, so his low-frequency loss points to the apex.
whyNot: This is left conductive hearing loss, as from cerumen, otitis media, or otosclerosis. His loss is sensorineural with normal tympanic membranes.
Bilateral negative Rinne tests with a midline Weber suggest symmetric conductive loss. His loss is one-sided and sensorineural.
Weber lateralizes to the affected ear in conductive loss, not in sensorineural loss.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the same clinic because of 3 days of continuous, severe vertigo with nausea that began 1 week after an upper respiratory infection. The vertigo is worse with head movement but never stops. She has horizontal nystagmus beating to the right. Audiometry is normal, and there are no other neurologic findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vestibular neuritis
Viral labyrinthitis
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Meniere disease
approach: Sort peripheral vertigo by duration: seconds (positional vertigo), hours (Meniere disease), or days (neuritis or labyrinthitis).
Continuous vertigo for days after a viral illness points to inflammation of the vestibular nerve or labyrinth.
Normal hearing places the problem in the vestibular nerve alone.
questions.why: Vestibular neuritis is inflammation of the vestibular nerve, thought to be viral, possibly from reactivated herpes simplex virus type 1. It causes sudden continuous vertigo lasting days, nausea, and horizontal nystagmus beating away from the affected side, with normal hearing. Labyrinthitis involves the inner ear itself, so hearing loss and tinnitus come with the vertigo. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo comes from displaced otoconia, usually in the posterior semicircular canal, and causes brief vertigo with head position changes and a positive Dix-Hallpike test.
whyNot: Correct.
Labyrinthitis affects the cochlea as well as the vestibular organs, so it causes hearing loss. Her audiometry is normal.
Positional vertigo lasts less than a minute with each change in head position. Her vertigo is continuous for days.
Meniere disease causes recurrent episodes lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and fullness.

questions.stem: His vertigo becomes disabling, and section of the left vestibular nerve is planned. The surgeon must protect a second cranial nerve that passes through the same bony canal. Injury to that nerve would most likely cause which of the following?
options: Loss of the gag reflex with hoarseness
Weakness of the whole ipsilateral face
Tongue deviation toward the injured side
Weak jaw closure on the injured side
approach: The vestibular nerve, part of CN VIII, leaves the posterior cranial fossa through the internal acoustic meatus.
The facial nerve (CN VII) travels with it through the internal acoustic meatus.
Injury there causes lower motor neuron weakness of the entire face on that side.
questions.why: The internal acoustic meatus carries the facial nerve (CN VII) and the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), along with the labyrinthine artery. Damage to the facial nerve at this level paralyzes all the muscles of facial expression on that side, including the forehead, and can also reduce taste, tearing, and the stapedius reflex. A central lesion above the facial nucleus spares the forehead because the upper face receives cortical input from both hemispheres.
whyNot: Loss of the gag reflex with hoarseness points to CN IX and CN X, which leave through the jugular foramen.
Correct.
Tongue deviation toward the lesion comes from CN XII injury. That nerve leaves through the hypoglossal canal.
Weak jaw closure comes from injury to the motor root of CN V3, which leaves through the foramen ovale.

case: A 74-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because of a 1-year history of difficulty walking and a 6-month history of urinary urgency with incontinence. She says he has become slow in his thinking and less interested in his hobbies. Physical examination shows a wide-based gait with short steps in which his feet seem stuck to the floor. There is no tremor, and tone in the arms is normal. Mini-Mental State Examination score is 23/30. MRI of the brain shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles out of proportion to sulcal enlargement, with no obstructing mass. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 15 cm H2O (normal about 10 to 20). His gait improves after removal of 40 mL of cerebrospinal fluid. Diagnosis: normal pressure hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his gait disturbance and urinary incontinence?
options: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine neurons in the midbrain
Stretched periventricular fibers from medial frontal cortex
Compression of the cerebellar vermis by the fourth ventricle
Degeneration of sacral parasympathetic preganglionic neurons
approach: Link his triad (gait disturbance, incontinence, cognitive decline) to enlarged lateral ventricles.
Recall which fibers lie next to the lateral ventricles: descending fibers from the medial frontal cortex that control the legs and bladder.
The enlarged ventricles stretch these fibers, so leg control and bladder inhibition suffer first.
questions.why: In normal pressure hydrocephalus, CSF absorption is impaired, the ventricles enlarge, and the opening pressure is usually normal or only intermittently high. The enlarged lateral ventricles stretch nearby white matter of the corona radiata. Fibers from the medial frontal cortex and paracentral lobule, which control the legs and inhibit the bladder, run closest to the ventricle walls, so a magnetic gait and urge incontinence come early, followed by frontal slowing of thought. Symptoms that improve after a large-volume CSF tap suggest a shunt may help.
whyNot: Nigral loss causes Parkinson disease, with resting tremor and rigidity. His tone is normal and he has no tremor.
Correct.
His MRI shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles. Vermis compression would cause truncal ataxia and would not explain incontinence.
Sacral parasympathetic damage, as in cauda equina syndrome, causes urinary retention with overflow and saddle anesthesia, not urge incontinence with a magnetic gait.

questions.stem: For the CSF removal, a needle is inserted in the midline between the spinous processes at the level of a line joining the highest points of the iliac crests. When CSF flows from the needle, its tip lies within which of the following spaces?
options: Lumbar cistern containing the cauda equina
Epidural space containing the vertebral venous plexus
Subdural space between dura and arachnoid
Central canal of the conus medullaris
approach: The line joining the iliac crests crosses at about the L4 spinous process.
In adults the spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris near L1 to L2, so the needle at L3 to L5 enters below the cord.
Below the conus, the subarachnoid space widens into the lumbar cistern, filled with CSF and nerve roots of the cauda equina.
questions.why: Lumbar puncture is done at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5, below the end of the spinal cord. The needle passes skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, the epidural space, dura, and arachnoid, then enters the lumbar cistern, an enlarged part of the subarachnoid space. The floating roots of the cauda equina usually slide away from the needle. CSF is normally returned to venous blood through arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses, mainly the superior sagittal sinus.
whyNot: Correct.
The epidural space contains fat and the vertebral venous plexus. No CSF flows from it, and it is where epidural anesthetic is placed.
The subdural space is only a potential space and holds no free CSF. Injecting into it by mistake is a known complication.
The conus medullaris lies above the puncture level, at about L1 to L2 in adults, and its central canal is too small to tap.

questions.stem: Before his MRI, his physician considered other causes of cognitive decline. Which of the following features would most strongly favor vascular dementia over Alzheimer disease?
options: Gradual early loss of recent memory with normal gait
Recurrent visual hallucinations with fluctuating alertness
Early disinhibition and personality change with spared memory
Stepwise decline with focal neurologic signs
approach: Recall the course of Alzheimer disease: slow, steady decline that starts with recent memory.
Vascular dementia follows strokes or diffuse small vessel disease, so it often worsens in steps and comes with focal signs.
Match the other options to Lewy body and frontotemporal dementia.
questions.why: Vascular dementia results from multiple infarcts or diffuse small vessel ischemia, usually in patients with hypertension, diabetes, or smoking. Its course is often stepwise, with sudden drops after new infarcts, and exam may show focal weakness, reflex changes, or gait problems. Alzheimer disease declines gradually and begins with trouble forming new memories. Mild cognitive impairment is measurable decline in memory or another domain with daily function still preserved, and it may progress to dementia.
whyNot: Slow, steady loss of recent memory with normal gait and no focal signs is the classic picture of Alzheimer disease.
Visual hallucinations with fluctuating alertness suggest dementia with Lewy bodies.
Early disinhibition and personality change with relatively spared memory suggest frontotemporal dementia.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman in the same clinic has pain and numbness in both buttocks and legs after walking about two blocks. The symptoms ease within minutes when she sits or leans forward on a shopping cart, and she can ride a stationary bicycle without pain. Pedal pulses are normal. Which of the following best explains why bending forward relieves her symptoms?
options: Flexion increases arterial inflow to calf muscles
Flexion lowers pressure within the intervertebral disc
Flexion widens the canal and eases cauda equina compression
Flexion relaxes the piriformis muscle over the sciatic nerve
approach: Recognize neurogenic claudication: leg symptoms with standing and walking, relieved by sitting or flexing forward, with normal pulses.
Recall that lumbar spinal stenosis narrows the canal through disc bulging, facet hypertrophy, and a thickened ligamentum flavum.
Extension narrows the canal further, and flexion opens it, which relieves pressure on the nerve roots.
questions.why: Lumbar spinal stenosis, usually from degenerative change in older adults, narrows the central canal and lateral recesses. In extension, as in standing and walking upright, the ligamentum flavum buckles inward and the canal shrinks, compressing the cauda equina. Flexion enlarges the canal, so symptoms ease with sitting, leaning on a cart, cycling, or walking uphill. Vascular claudication, by contrast, is relieved by simply stopping and comes with weak pulses. Cervical stenosis compresses the cord itself and causes myelopathy with upper motor neuron signs.
whyNot: Vascular claudication depends on blood flow, so it is relieved by stopping activity regardless of posture, and pulses are weak. Her pulses are normal and cycling does not hurt.
Flexion raises intradiscal pressure, which is why disc herniation pain often worsens with sitting and bending.
Correct.
Piriformis syndrome causes buttock pain with sitting and hip rotation. It does not cause bilateral leg symptoms with walking.

case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 3 months of daily headaches that are worse in the morning and when lying down. She has brief episodes of vision going gray when she stands up, a whooshing sound in both ears, and horizontal double vision at distance. She began taking minocycline for acne 4 months ago. Body mass index is 38 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral optic disc swelling. Her left eye does not abduct fully. Visual field testing shows enlarged blind spots. MRI of the brain and MR venography are normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 34 cm H2O (normal about 10 to 20) with normal CSF composition. Diagnosis: idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her double vision?
options: Compression of the oculomotor nerve by the uncus
A demyelinating lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus
Inflammation of the lateral rectus muscle
Stretch of the abducens nerve over the petrous apex
approach: Localize the deficit: failed abduction of the left eye means a CN VI problem.
Recall that CN VI has a long course along the clivus and over the petrous apex, where raised pressure can stretch it.
In raised intracranial pressure, a CN VI palsy is a false localizing sign; it does not mark the site of a lesion.
questions.why: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects obese women of childbearing age. Raised CSF pressure causes headache, papilledema, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, and sometimes a CN VI palsy, while imaging shows no mass and no venous sinus thrombosis. The abducens nerve is vulnerable because it runs a long path up the clivus and bends over the petrous apex. Known triggers include tetracyclines such as minocycline and excess vitamin A or retinoids. The main danger is permanent vision loss from chronic papilledema.
whyNot: Uncal herniation compresses CN III, giving a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye. She has normal imaging and failed abduction.
A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion impairs adduction, not abduction, and her MRI shows no demyelinating lesion.
Lateral rectus myositis is painful and would not explain papilledema or a raised opening pressure.
Correct.

questions.stem: Despite treatment, chronic papilledema leads to complete atrophy of the left optic nerve, while the right optic nerve recovers. Which of the following visual field defects is most likely?
options: Right homonymous hemianopia
Bitemporal heteronymous hemianopia
Left monocular blindness
Right superior quadrantanopia
approach: Place the lesion: the left optic nerve, in front of the chiasm.
Before the chiasm, each optic nerve carries all fibers from one eye.
So a complete left optic nerve lesion blinds the left eye and spares the right.
questions.why: Fibers from each retina travel in that eye's optic nerve to the chiasm, where the nasal fibers cross. Behind the chiasm, each optic tract carries the opposite visual field from both eyes. A lesion of one optic nerve causes loss of vision in that eye. A chiasm lesion causes bitemporal hemianopia. A lesion of the optic tract or the whole radiation causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia. A lesion of the Meyer loop in the temporal lobe causes contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
whyNot: Right homonymous hemianopia comes from a lesion behind the chiasm on the left, such as the left optic tract, radiation, or occipital cortex.
Bitemporal hemianopia comes from a lesion of the crossing fibers at the chiasm, classically a pituitary adenoma.
Correct.
Right superior quadrantanopia comes from a lesion of the left Meyer loop in the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: She is treated with acetazolamide, which inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the cells that secrete CSF. Which of the following forms the barrier between blood and CSF at this site?
options: Brain capillary endothelium sealed by tight junctions
Choroid plexus epithelium sealed by tight junctions
Fenestrated endothelium of the area postrema
Arachnoid barrier cells beneath the dura
approach: CSF is secreted by the choroid plexus in the ventricles.
Choroid plexus capillaries are fenestrated and leaky, so the barrier must lie in the epithelium covering them.
Tight junctions between choroid plexus epithelial cells form the blood-CSF barrier.
questions.why: The blood-brain barrier is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells joined by tight junctions, supported by their basement membrane and astrocyte foot processes. The blood-CSF barrier is in a different place: choroid plexus capillaries are fenestrated, and the barrier is formed by tight junctions between the choroid plexus epithelial cells, which secrete CSF. Carbonic anhydrase in these cells supplies bicarbonate and drives sodium and water secretion, so acetazolamide lowers CSF production. Circumventricular organs such as the area postrema and posterior pituitary lack a barrier so they can sense or release substances in the blood.
whyNot: Brain capillary endothelium forms the blood-brain barrier between blood and brain tissue, not the barrier at the site of CSF secretion.
Correct.
The area postrema lacks a barrier, which lets it detect toxins in blood and trigger vomiting. It does not secrete CSF.
The arachnoid barrier layer separates the dura from CSF in the subarachnoid space. It is not where CSF is made.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who delivered a baby 10 days ago develops a severe headache, papilledema, and a seizure. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. MRI shows hemorrhagic infarcts in the parasagittal cortex of both hemispheres that do not follow an arterial territory. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus
Rupture of a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis
Hypertensive vasogenic edema of posterior white matter
Embolic occlusion of the middle cerebral artery
approach: The postpartum state is hypercoagulable.
Bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic infarcts outside arterial territories point to blocked venous drainage into the superior sagittal sinus.
Blocked venous outflow also impairs CSF absorption, which raises intracranial pressure and causes papilledema.
questions.why: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis occurs in hypercoagulable states such as pregnancy and the postpartum period, estrogen use, and inherited thrombophilias. When the superior sagittal sinus clots, venous pressure rises in the cortex it drains, causing edema and hemorrhagic venous infarcts in both parasagittal regions. CSF absorption through the arachnoid granulations also falls, so pressure rises. It can mimic idiopathic intracranial hypertension, which is why MR venography is done. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, by contrast, is vasogenic edema of posterior white matter during severe hypertension.
whyNot: Correct.
Aneurysm rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage with a sudden worst headache, not bilateral parasagittal infarcts.
Vasogenic edema of posterior white matter describes posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, which usually occurs with severe hypertension or eclampsia. Her blood pressure is normal.
A middle cerebral artery embolus causes a single infarct in that arterial territory on one side, not bilateral parasagittal lesions.

case: A 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of 2 days of confusion and daytime sleepiness. He has passed black stools since yesterday. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. He is jaundiced and disoriented to time. Examination shows spider angiomas, ascites, and a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. Rectal examination shows melena. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), sodium 124 mEq/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.1 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), and venous ammonia 112 µmol/L (about 10 to 40). Diagnosis: hepatic encephalopathy in alcoholic cirrhosis, precipitated by upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how the bleeding precipitated his encephalopathy?
options: Blood loss reduced cerebral perfusion below autoregulatory limits
Bilirubin from hemoglobin breakdown crossed the blood-brain barrier
Bacteria digested blood protein, and the ammonia bypassed the liver
Iron from hemoglobin generated free radicals in the basal ganglia
approach: Blood in the gut is a large protein load.
Colonic bacteria break down that protein and release ammonia, which is absorbed into the portal blood.
In cirrhosis with portosystemic shunting, the ammonia reaches the brain without being cleared by the liver.
questions.why: Normally the liver removes gut-derived ammonia through the urea cycle. In cirrhosis, hepatocyte function is reduced, and portal blood flows through portosystemic shunts straight into the systemic circulation, so ammonia and other gut toxins reach the brain. Anything that raises ammonia production or absorption can tip a patient into encephalopathy: gastrointestinal bleeding, high protein intake, constipation, infection, and hypokalemia, which increases renal ammonia production. Confusion, sleep-wake reversal, and asterixis are the typical signs. Lactulose and rifaximin reduce ammonia production and absorption.
whyNot: His blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg, within the autoregulatory range. Low perfusion would not raise his ammonia.
Bilirubin enters the brain mainly in newborns, causing kernicterus. It does not cause encephalopathy in adult cirrhosis.
Correct.
Iron and free radical injury are not the mechanism of hepatic encephalopathy. Iron deposits in the basal ganglia occur in other disorders.

questions.stem: Brain tissue from a patient who died of this disorder shows astrocytes with enlarged, pale nuclei (Alzheimer type II astrocytes). Which of the following reactions in these cells best explains their swelling?
options: Glutamate plus ammonia forming glutamine
Glutamine hydrolysis releasing ammonia
Alpha-ketoglutarate transamination forming glutamate
Ornithine plus carbamoyl phosphate forming citrulline
approach: The brain has no urea cycle, so it detoxifies ammonia by another route.
Astrocytes use glutamine synthetase to combine ammonia with glutamate, forming glutamine.
Glutamine builds up inside astrocytes, draws in water osmotically, and the cells swell.
questions.why: Astrocytes are the main cells in the brain that remove ammonia. Glutamine synthetase, an ATP-dependent enzyme, joins ammonia to glutamate to make glutamine. With high ammonia, glutamine accumulates in astrocytes, pulls water in, and the cells swell, which contributes to brain edema. The swollen astrocytes with large pale nuclei are called Alzheimer type II astrocytes. Ammonia also depletes glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate, which disrupts neurotransmission and the TCA cycle in brain cells. Urea cycle enzyme defects cause the same brain injury in infants.
whyNot: Correct.
Glutaminase releases ammonia from glutamine, mainly in the kidney and gut. That reaction would add to the ammonia load, not trap it.
Transamination moves an amino group between molecules but does not remove free ammonia, so it does not explain glutamine buildup.
This is a urea cycle step that occurs in liver mitochondria. The brain lacks a working urea cycle.

questions.stem: His serum sodium is raised from 124 mEq/L to 136 mEq/L within 24 hours. Three days later, he develops slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, and weakness of all four limbs. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his new findings?
options: Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine depletion
Worsening hepatic encephalopathy from new bleeding
Cerebral edema from rapid water shift into neurons
Demyelination of the central basis pontis
approach: Note the rise in sodium: 12 mEq/L in 24 hours, above the safe limit of about 8 mEq/L per day for a high-risk patient like him (about 10 to 12 for others).
In chronic hyponatremia, brain cells have shed solutes to avoid swelling; rapid correction pulls water out of them.
Glial cells in the central pons are injured, causing dysarthria, dysphagia, and quadriparesis a few days later.
questions.why: In chronic hyponatremia, brain cells lose organic osmolytes to stay at normal volume. When sodium is corrected too quickly, water leaves the cells, and oligodendrocytes are injured, especially in the central basis pontis. This causes osmotic demyelination syndrome, which appears 2 to 6 days after correction with dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, and in severe cases locked-in syndrome. Alcohol use, malnutrition, liver disease, and hypokalemia raise the risk, so the correction limit is lower in patients like him.
whyNot: Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. It does not cause dysarthria and quadriparesis after sodium correction.
Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion and asterixis, not new quadriparesis with bulbar weakness.
Raising sodium moves water out of brain cells, so cells shrink. Cerebral edema results when hypernatremia is corrected too quickly.
Correct.

questions.stem: Early in his illness, his wife noticed that he slept during the day and was awake at night. Which of the following normally keeps the sleep-wake cycle aligned with daylight?
options: Retinal light input increasing melatonin secretion during the day
Suprachiasmatic nucleus timing nightly pineal melatonin release
Lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons secreting melatonin at night
Ventromedial nucleus timing nightly adrenal cortisol release
approach: Identify the master clock: the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
It receives light information directly from the retina through the retinohypothalamic tract.
It controls the pineal gland through a sympathetic pathway, so melatonin rises in darkness and falls in light.
questions.why: The suprachiasmatic nucleus sits just above the optic chiasm and keeps a roughly 24-hour rhythm. Light reaching special retinal ganglion cells is relayed to it by the retinohypothalamic tract, which resets the clock each day. The nucleus signals the pineal gland through a pathway that passes through the superior cervical ganglion, and the pineal secretes melatonin at night, promoting sleep. Orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus keep a person awake, and their loss causes narcolepsy with cataplexy.
whyNot: Light suppresses melatonin. Melatonin is high at night and low during the day.
Correct.
Orexin neurons promote wakefulness and do not secrete melatonin. Their loss causes narcolepsy.
The ventromedial nucleus is a satiety center. Cortisol peaks in the early morning, but it is not the signal that sets the sleep cycle.

case: A 63-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of 2 years of burning pain and numbness in her feet that now reach just below the knees, with recent tingling in her fingertips. She also reports early satiety and lightheadedness when she stands. Her hemoglobin A1c is 9.4% (goal less than 7). Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg supine and 98/64 mm Hg standing, with no change in pulse. Examination shows decreased pinprick, vibration, and position sense in a stocking-and-glove distribution and absent ankle reflexes. There is a painless ulcer under the first metatarsal head of the right foot. Nerve conduction studies show reduced sensory and motor response amplitudes with nearly normal conduction velocities. Diagnosis: distal symmetric diabetic polyneuropathy.

questions.stem: Persistent hyperglycemia damages her nerves partly through an enzyme in Schwann cells that converts excess intracellular glucose to an osmotically active alcohol, using NADPH. Which of the following enzymes is this?
options: Aldose reductase
Glucokinase
Galactokinase
Sorbitol dehydrogenase
approach: Schwann cells take up glucose without insulin, so their glucose rises with blood glucose.
Aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol using NADPH.
Sorbitol is trapped in the cell, draws in water, and NADPH depletion weakens antioxidant defense.
questions.why: In the polyol pathway, aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, and sorbitol dehydrogenase converts sorbitol to fructose. Schwann cells, the lens, and the retina have little sorbitol dehydrogenase, so sorbitol accumulates, causing osmotic injury. Using up NADPH lowers glutathione regeneration and leaves cells exposed to oxidative stress. Advanced glycation end products and damage to the small vessels that supply nerves add to the injury. The results include stocking-and-glove sensory loss, autonomic dysfunction such as gastroparesis and orthostatic hypotension, neuropathic foot ulcers, and pupil-sparing CN III palsy from nerve infarction.
whyNot: Correct.
Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose in liver and pancreatic beta cells. It does not form sorbitol.
Galactokinase phosphorylates galactose. Its deficiency causes galactitol cataracts in infants.
Sorbitol dehydrogenase removes sorbitol by converting it to fructose. It is scarce in Schwann cells, which is why sorbitol builds up.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the pattern and type of her nerve injury?
options: Mononeuritis multiplex from vasculitic nerve infarcts
Acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy
Single compressive mononeuropathy of the tibial nerve
Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy
approach: Pattern: symmetric loss that starts in the feet and later reaches the fingertips, the longest nerves first.
Type: reduced response amplitudes with nearly normal conduction velocity means axons are lost while remaining myelin is intact.
Put them together: a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy.
questions.why: Peripheral neuropathy is sorted by pattern and by the part of the nerve injured. A distal symmetric polyneuropathy hits the longest axons first, so it begins in the toes and reaches the fingertips once leg symptoms are near the knees. Axonal injury lowers response amplitudes, while demyelination slows conduction and causes conduction block. Diabetes is the most common cause of distal symmetric axonal neuropathy. Others include alcohol, B12 and thiamine deficiency, HIV, and neurotoxic chemotherapy. Mononeuritis multiplex, with separate nerves hit in sequence, suggests vasculitis, and leprosy causes patchy sensory loss in cool skin.
whyNot: Mononeuritis multiplex affects separate named nerves in a patchy, stepwise pattern. Her loss is symmetric and length-dependent.
An acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, Guillain-Barre syndrome, develops over days and shows slowed conduction velocities. Her course is 2 years with near-normal velocities.
A single tibial nerve lesion would not explain symmetric loss in both feet and the hands.
Correct.

questions.stem: A sural nerve biopsy is stained for the tight junction protein claudin-1. A continuous ring of thin, flattened cells around each fascicle stains strongly. Which of the following layers has been stained?
options: Epineurium
Perineurium
Endoneurium
Schwann cell basal lamina
approach: Recall the three connective tissue layers: endoneurium around each axon, perineurium around each fascicle, epineurium around the whole nerve.
The layer that wraps each fascicle is the perineurium.
Its cells are joined by tight junctions, so it forms the diffusion barrier of the blood-nerve barrier.
questions.why: A peripheral nerve is built in layers. Endoneurium is loose connective tissue around each nerve fiber. Perineurium surrounds each fascicle and is made of layers of flattened cells joined by tight junctions with a basal lamina on each side. Epineurium is dense connective tissue that wraps the whole nerve and its blood vessels. The perineurium, together with tight junctions in endoneurial capillaries, forms the blood-nerve barrier that keeps the endoneurial fluid stable around axons.
whyNot: Epineurium is dense irregular connective tissue around the whole nerve. It does not form a ring of tight-junction cells around each fascicle.
Correct.
Endoneurium is loose connective tissue around individual nerve fibers inside a fascicle.
The Schwann cell basal lamina surrounds each nerve fiber, not each fascicle, and is extracellular matrix, not a layer of cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on funduscopic examination of this patient?
options: Arteriovenous nicking with copper-wire arteriolar reflexes
Bilateral optic disc swelling with blurred margins
Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, and hard exudates
Cherry-red fovea within a pale, edematous retina
approach: Long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes causing neuropathy also damages small vessels in the retina.
The first retinal changes of diabetes are microaneurysms from capillary wall weakness, with leaks that leave hemorrhages and lipid exudates.
Match the other options to hypertension, raised intracranial pressure, and arterial occlusion.
questions.why: Diabetic retinopathy begins as nonproliferative disease, with pericyte loss, basement membrane thickening, microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, and hard exudates from leaky capillaries. Retinal ischemia then drives VEGF release and neovascularization, which defines proliferative disease and can bleed or detach the retina. Hypertensive retinopathy shows arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, and cotton wool spots. Papilledema is swelling of both optic discs from raised intracranial pressure.
whyNot: AV nicking and copper-wire arterioles are signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Her blood pressure is normal.
Bilateral optic disc swelling is papilledema from raised intracranial pressure, which nothing in her case suggests.
Correct.
A cherry-red fovea with a pale, swollen retina is the picture of central retinal artery occlusion, which causes sudden painless vision loss.

dx: Subacute combined degeneration from pernicious anemia (vitamin B12 deficiency)
case: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of 5 months of tingling in his feet and hands, unsteadiness when walking in the dark, and forgetfulness. He has autoimmune hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Examination shows a smooth, red tongue. Vibration and joint position sense are reduced in both feet, and Romberg sign is positive. Muscle tone is increased in the legs, knee reflexes are brisk, ankle reflexes are absent, and plantar responses are extensor on both sides. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), mean corpuscular volume 112 fL (80 to 100), hypersegmented neutrophils, and serum vitamin B12 140 pg/mL (about 200 to 900). Antibodies to intrinsic factor are present. Diagnosis: subacute combined degeneration from pernicious anemia.

questions.stem: His daughter asks why his diet, which includes meat and dairy daily, did not prevent the deficiency. Which of the following best explains his deficiency?
options: Failure of pancreatic proteases to free cobalamin from haptocorrin
Competition for cobalamin by an intestinal tapeworm
Loss of receptor-mediated uptake in a diseased ileum
Loss of the gastric protein needed for ileal uptake
approach: Recall the B12 absorption steps: release from food in the stomach, binding to haptocorrin, release by pancreatic proteases, binding to intrinsic factor, uptake in the terminal ileum.
Pernicious anemia is autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells, which make intrinsic factor.
Without intrinsic factor, dietary B12 cannot be taken up in the ileum, however much he eats.
questions.why: Pernicious anemia is the most common cause of B12 deficiency in adults. Autoantibodies and T cells destroy parietal cells in the gastric body and fundus, and antibodies to intrinsic factor block the vitamin from binding it, so B12 is not absorbed in the terminal ileum. It often occurs with other autoimmune diseases such as autoimmune thyroiditis. Other causes of B12 deficiency include a strict vegan diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease or resection, and the fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum. Neurologic findings include subacute combined degeneration, peripheral neuropathy, and dementia.
whyNot: Pancreatic insufficiency can impair B12 release from haptocorrin, but nothing suggests pancreatic disease, and intrinsic factor antibodies point to the stomach.
Diphyllobothrium latum competes for B12 in people who eat raw freshwater fish. His intrinsic factor antibodies explain the deficiency.
Crohn disease or resection of the terminal ileum removes the site of uptake. His ileum is not reported as diseased, and the antibodies point to intrinsic factor.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of laboratory results would best confirm vitamin B12 deficiency, rather than folate deficiency, as the cause of his megaloblastic anemia?
options: Elevated homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid
Elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid
Normal homocysteine with elevated methylmalonic acid
Normal homocysteine and methylmalonic acid
approach: B12 is the cofactor for two enzymes: methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
Loss of methionine synthase raises homocysteine in both B12 and folate deficiency.
Only B12 deficiency also blocks methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so methylmalonic acid rises as well.
questions.why: Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to move a methyl group from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, forming methionine and regenerating tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis. Deficiency of either B12 or folate stalls this step, raises homocysteine, and causes megaloblastic anemia. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses adenosylcobalamin to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, and it needs B12 only. Its failure raises methylmalonic acid and leads to abnormal fatty acids in myelin, and reduced S-adenosylmethionine impairs myelin methylation. This is why B12 deficiency damages the nervous system and folate deficiency does not.
whyNot: This pattern fits folate deficiency, which blocks methionine synthase but leaves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase working.
Correct.
A B12 deficiency severe enough to cause anemia also blocks methionine synthase, so homocysteine would be high too.
Normal levels of both would argue against deficiency of either vitamin as the cause of his anemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of spinal cord structures is most affected in this patient?
options: Dorsal columns and dorsal roots
Lateral spinothalamic tracts and anterior horns
Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Anterior horns and lateral corticospinal tracts
approach: Lost vibration and position sense with a positive Romberg sign points to the dorsal columns.
Spasticity, brisk knee reflexes, and extensor plantar responses point to the lateral corticospinal tracts.
Both tracts together, from B12 deficiency, is subacute combined degeneration. The absent ankle reflexes come from the accompanying peripheral neuropathy.
questions.why: Subacute combined degeneration is demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, usually starting in the cervical and upper thoracic cord. Patients lose vibration and position sense, sway with eyes closed, and develop spastic weakness with extensor plantar responses. A coexisting peripheral neuropathy can abolish ankle reflexes. Tabes dorsalis affects dorsal columns and dorsal roots and gives sensory ataxia with lost reflexes but no upper motor neuron signs. Anterior spinal artery infarction spares the dorsal columns. Complete transection removes all function below the level.
whyNot: Dorsal column and dorsal root damage is tabes dorsalis from neurosyphilis. It lacks upper motor neuron signs such as extensor plantar responses.

Spinothalamic tract and anterior horn damage with the dorsal columns spared is anterior spinal artery infarction, which causes weakness and loss of pain and temperature with vibration and position sense preserved. His dorsal column function is lost.
Correct.
Anterior horn and corticospinal tract damage is ALS, which causes no sensory loss.

questions.stem: The loss of vibration and position sense in his feet reflects damage to which of the following tracts, and where do the second-order fibers of that pathway cross the midline?
options: Fasciculus gracilis, crossing in the caudal medulla
Fasciculus cuneatus, crossing in the caudal medulla
Fasciculus gracilis, crossing at the level of entry
Fasciculus cuneatus, crossing in the anterior white commissure
approach: Sensation from the legs ascends in the medial part of the dorsal columns, the fasciculus gracilis.
First-order fibers ascend on the same side and synapse in the nucleus gracilis in the medulla.
Second-order fibers cross there as internal arcuate fibers and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus.
questions.why: The dorsal column medial lemniscus pathway carries vibration, position sense, and fine touch. First-order axons enter the cord and ascend on the same side, leg fibers medially in the fasciculus gracilis and arm fibers laterally in the fasciculus cuneatus above T6. They synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the caudal medulla, and second-order fibers cross as internal arcuate fibers, rise in the medial lemniscus to the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, and project to the postcentral gyrus. A cord lesion therefore causes loss on the same side below the lesion. Pain and temperature cross within a segment or two of entry in the anterior white commissure, so a cord lesion causes loss on the opposite side.
whyNot: Correct.
The fasciculus cuneatus carries sensation from the upper body and arms, not the feet.
Fibers that cross near their level of entry belong to the spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature.
The fasciculus cuneatus carries arm sensation, and crossing in the anterior white commissure describes the spinothalamic tract.
